```{r setup}
library(multisiteDGP)
```

multisiteDGP simulates the summary data of a multisite trial: for each site, a
true effect, an estimate of that effect, and the standard error of the
estimate. This vignette runs one simulation from a preset and explains the
result: the columns, the printed header, the diagnostics, and two plots. It
then shows how to change the design and what a seed does.

## Installation

Install the package from GitHub with the remotes package.

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
remotes::install_github("joonho112/multisiteDGP")
```

## One simulation

A design is an object that holds the settings of a simulation, such as the
number of sites, the distribution of the site effects, and the site sizes. A
preset is a function that returns a complete design.
`preset_education_modest()` returns a design with 50 sites, normal site
effects with mean 0 and cross-site standard deviation 0.2, and site sizes that
average 50. The outcome has variance 1, so effects are in standard deviation
units. `sim_multisite()` simulates one data set from a design.

```{r simulate}
dat <- sim_multisite(preset_education_modest(), seed = 1)
dat
```

The first four lines are a header written by the package. Below them is a
tibble with one row per site.

## The simulated data

The tibble has seven columns.

| Column | Content |
|--------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| `site_index` | site number |
| `z_j` | standardized site effect, with mean 0 and variance 1 in the population |
| `tau_j` | site effect, $\tau_j = \tau + \sigma_\tau z_j$, with grand mean $\tau$ and cross-site standard deviation $\sigma_\tau$ |
| `tau_j_hat` | observed estimate, drawn from a normal distribution with mean `tau_j` and variance `se2_j` |
| `se_j` | standard error of the estimate |
| `se2_j` | sampling variance, the square of `se_j` |
| `n_j` | site size, the number of individuals in the site |

A real trial provides only `tau_j_hat`, `se_j`, and `n_j`. The columns `z_j`
and `tau_j` are the truth that a simulation study compares its estimates with.
The standard errors come from the site sizes. Site 4, with 12 individuals, has
a standard error of 0.577, and site 6, with 68, has 0.243.

The first header line gives the number of sites, the source of the standard
errors, and the seed. The `sigma_tau` line sets the cross-site standard
deviation in the design (0.200) against the standard deviation of the 50
simulated site effects (0.166). The next line does the same for the rank
correlation between site effects and standard errors. The design asks for
none, and these 50 sites happen to have 0.254. The last line is the
informativeness $I$, the share of the variance of a typical site's estimate
that comes from the site effects and not from sampling error.

`summary()` prints the diagnostics stored in `attr(dat, "diagnostics")`, in
four blocks.

```{r summary}
summary(dat)
```

Each row gives the value realized in this data set, the target if the design
sets one, and a status if a rule applies to the row. The blocks describe the
scale of the site effects and the sampling variances, the dependence between
them, the shape of the effect distribution, and how well single sites can be
estimated. `vignette("diagnostics-and-presets")` explains every row.

In the first three blocks a status compares this one data set with its
design, and the rule allows for the sampling error of 50 sites. The
`sigma_tau` row passes although the realized 0.166 is 17 percent below the
target of 0.200, because the standard deviation of 50 draws has a standard
error of about 10 percent of its value. A data set simulated from this design
passes each of the three rows about 95 times in 100, so a `warn` on one of
them is usually chance. In the precision block a status describes the design.
The average margin of error, 1.96 times the average standard error, is 0.617.
That is three times the cross-site standard deviation, so single sites are
estimated with little precision, and the row is marked `warn`.

## Plots

`plot_effects()` draws the estimates in increasing order with their 95 percent
intervals, and adds the site effects as a second set of points.

```{r effects, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "The estimates with their 95 percent intervals (green) spread far more widely than the site effects (orange)."}
plot_effects(dat)
```

From bottom to top the green points move from about $-0.7$ to 0.6, and the
orange points rise much less. Site 41, at the bottom, has the lowest estimate,
and its site effect is close to zero. Most of the spread in the estimates is
sampling error, which is what an informativeness of 0.303 means. The subtitle
repeats four numbers from `summary()`: the number of sites, the
informativeness, the heterogeneity ratio, and the rank correlation.

`plot_funnel()` plots the standard error of each site against its estimate,
with the most precise sites at the top.

```{r funnel, fig.cap = "Nearly all estimates lie between the dotted lines, which are 1.96 standard errors either side of zero."}
plot_funnel(dat)
```

The estimates scatter on both sides of the dashed line at every standard
error, as expected from a design without dependence between effects and
precision. Both functions return a ggplot object, so layers and labels can be
added with `+`.

## Changing the design

Arguments given to a preset replace the preset's values.

```{r override}
design <- preset_education_modest(J = 100, nj_mean = 200)
design
```

The `J` line now reads 100 sites and the `nj_mean` line reads 200. All other
values are those of the preset.

```{r override-sim}
sim_multisite(design, seed = 1)
```

The header shows 100 sites and an informativeness of 0.659, up from 0.303.
Sites that are four times as large have sampling variances about a quarter the
size.

`multisitedgp_design()` builds a design without a preset. Every argument has a
default, so only the values that differ need to be given. `sim_multisite()`
also takes the same arguments directly.

```{r direct}
design <- multisitedgp_design(J = 30, sigma_tau = 0.15, nj_mean = 80)
identical(
  sim_multisite(design, seed = 1),
  sim_multisite(J = 30, sigma_tau = 0.15, nj_mean = 80, seed = 1)
)
```

The two calls return the same data. A call takes either a design or design
arguments, not both. `update_multisitedgp_design()` returns a changed copy of
an existing design. `sim_meta()` sets the standard errors directly, from a
target informativeness `I` and a heterogeneity ratio `R`, instead of deriving
them from site sizes.

## Seeds

With a seed, the same call returns the same data in any R session. The
function seeds the random number generator for the simulation and, on exit,
restores the generator of your session to the state it was in. The seed is
stored with the data, in `attr(dat, "design")$seed`.

```{r seeds}
set.seed(1)
state <- .Random.seed
again <- sim_multisite(preset_education_modest(), seed = 1)
identical(again, dat)
identical(.Random.seed, state)
unseeded <- sim_multisite(preset_education_modest())
identical(.Random.seed, state)
```

The first two results are `TRUE`. The seeded call reproduces `dat`, and the
generator of your session is where `set.seed(1)` left it. Without a seed,
`sim_multisite()` draws from that generator, as `rnorm()` does. The third
result is `FALSE` because the unseeded call moved the generator forward, and
its data depend on the state the session was in.
